instruction:
Hey..Here's the plan: we will create a nice 30s scene of the pampa lake from valimiki ramayana.

Now, for that use the rive-cli and get the rive canvas into the code and then in turn use to render our video.

the rive files are in Documents>rive-cli>pampa-lake
activity: I've built the 30-second Pampā Sarovar scene, and your Rive lake now plays live
message:
I've built the 30-second Pampā Sarovar scene, and your Rive lake now plays live in the video. It fades up from dark on the still lake with the title "Pampā Sarovar" (marked as from Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa). The file's own camera move then glides over the water toward the lotus beds and the hamsas. Two short lines fade in over the water along the way ("Clear water, lotuses in bloom…" and "Here, in the spring, Rāma stood at the shore and longed for Sītā"), then it fades back to dark.

- **Which Rive file I used:** the one in `pampa-lake/web`, not a fresh build from the Rive CLI. The CLI's notes say local builds carry unsigned scripts, which web players refuse, so I used the copy your web page already plays. It's copied into the project's assets.
- **Same picture every time:** Rive's own clock is switched off and the video's time drives the scene. The same moment rendered twice came out effectively pixel-identical, including after jumping backwards in the timeline.
- **Words:** they're dark ink with a soft cream glow, because white text disappeared into the mist. Both lines are my paraphrase of the passage, not a quoted translation.
- **What the video needs to play:** the Rive player loads from the internet when the video previews or renders.
- **Other changes:** HyperFrames' own check passes. I updated the project's HyperFrames version from 0.8.151 to 0.9.16 and confirmed it still works.

The video has no sound yet. Want me to look for a soft music bed with birdsong and water to go under it?

log.text:
I'm weighing a Rive setup with autoplay turned off, since the state machine would otherwise run on its own clock. Rendering to an arbitrary time means I'd need a way to stop the loop and possibly reset the artboard when the target time falls behind the current one, and I'm considering whether a full reinit or something simpler would do.

I'm now weighing whether to drive the camera directly from JavaScript through the view model, computing each input from the tour keys and a Hermite interpolation of time, so the tour's accumulating clock doesn't matter. The catch is that the water, wind, and pollen still depend on an accumulating internal time, which only stays correct for forward seeks, so backward scrubbing would need a reset.

I'm checking whether advancing the animation without drawing is cheap enough to step forward in small increments. Stepping from zero each time would give a path-independent result, though forward-only stepping should be close enough. For backward seeks, a full reset is the remaining option, and I'm weighing whether rebuilding the artboard would be too slow.

I'm considering whether a reset is needed for backward seeks, since the script's time can't be rewound. Editing and rebuilding the script would produce an unsigned file that web runtimes reject, so I'm leaning toward a full reset. I'll check whether `Rive.reset` exists for that.

Next I'll set up a headless browser check and copy the Rive runtime files into the project so rendering works offline. The story is the Pampa lake scene from the Kishkindha Kanda, with a 30-second duration.

I'm settling the on-screen text: a title card reading "Pampā Sarovar" with a subtle verse line, then a fade. For pacing, I'll set the tour speed so the 30-second run covers the full path from the hero view through the lotus beds to the hamsas, which works out to about 1.47. The opening still hold will then last around 2.7 seconds, enough for the title.

I'm checking the Lake script's ScriptInput defaults for `tour` in scene.rml, and I'll set `tour` and `tourSpeed` explicitly before the first advance. The data bindings only update during advance, so the values need to be in place before that. The script's drift sway runs off `self.time`, so it's unaffected. The canvas question is that the script's width and height inputs aren't bound to the view model, so the fixed 1280x720 artboard will need to be scaled up to 1920x1080 with fit-cover.

Next I'm checking whether the GPU canvas path will even run in a headless browser, since the scripted canvas relies on WebGL and might be slow under software rendering. I'll find out with a snapshot test, and I'm also wondering whether the deferred flush finishes before the screenshot is taken.

I'm checking the Rive API now, starting with whether `reset` takes the options I need and whether `advanceAndReportChanges` can step time without drawing. I also want to confirm the post-draw capture will pick up the frame from the seek handler.

I'm copying the Rive assets into the project folder and running a usage check, then I'll start writing the index.html layout: a 30-second root with the lake canvas full-bleed, a title overlay, and a verse line on separate tracks.

I'm setting up the text overlays on their timings: the title "Pampā Sarovar" with its eyebrow line around 2.5–8s, a paraphrased verse about Pampa's clear water and lotuses around 11–18s, and a closing line about Rāma longing for Sītā in spring around 21–27s. I'll also need local font files for Cormorant Garamond and DM Sans, and I'm checking how the Rive runtime's WASM path gets configured.

I'm wiring up the Rive runtime: the rive.js setup with the WASM URL, and the state machine needs to keep advancing even though I'm driving the frames myself rather than letting it run on its own loop.

I'm working out how to drive the Rive frames by hand: I'll clear and draw the artboard myself, then call the runtime's resolve step so the deferred flush actually runs, since the built-in render loop would restart on its own.

I'm working through how to take over the Rive rendering loop: the idea is to let the state machine keep advancing while stopping the runtime from scheduling its own frames, then call draw with a controlled timestamp myself and resolve the animation frame afterward so the deferred work actually flushes.

I'm wiring the Rive runtime to draw frames on a controlled clock: the state machine keeps advancing in fixed steps of up to 1/30 s, and I'll reset it and replay from zero whenever the requested time moves backward.

I'm adding a time guard so the Rive state machine steps forward in chunks no larger than 1/30 s, and the draw call itself gets a zero elapsed time so nothing else is advanced twice.

I'm checking how the state machine keeps advancing when I drive the frames myself, and whether advancing the script without drawing is safe. I'm also weighing a reset on backward seeks: it costs some scrubbing speed, but it keeps the output correct.

I'm checking whether the Rive constructor resizes the canvas by itself, since I'd rather set the 1920×1080 size explicitly and skip the device-pixel-ratio scaling.

I'm settling the Rive camera pacing: a tour speed of 1.6 gives about 48 seconds of tour, which covers the hero shot, the forward move, the lotus beds, and the curve toward the hamsas before the gaze lift, all settling under the fade.

I'm keeping the tour speed at 1.6 and leaving the other defaults alone, since the wind and water tuning were set on purpose. The water ripples, swans, and pollen already animate off time, so they'll move without extra settings. Next I'll check the RuntimeLoader fallback setter and the Rive parameter names, then write the files.
Rive's web runtime can be stepped by hand, so I'm now copying the signed lake file and runtime into the project and building the 30-second composition around it.

The stray draw calls look like the culprit: drawFrame goes straight to the internal draw with the document timeline's clock, so every one of them advances the script by up to 0.1s without my counter knowing. Rive's load sequence might also draw before onLoad, which would leave the script ahead of zero even after applyScene. I'm planning to route every draw through one function, stub out drawFrame, and call reset() on load so the state starts from exactly zero.

I'm going to make onLoad call reset() and then applyScene so the script starts from a clean zero, and I'm also checking whether draw itself goes through `_boundDraw`, since that would be another path the script could advance on.
Rive's `drawFrame` can still advance the scene by wall-clock time, which could make runs differ, so I'm locking that and starting from a clean reset.
